A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Easi3R. All pages, including Appendices A–D, are readable and support matching the text, equations, tables and figures. v2 retains the original work and adds supplementary evaluations.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 and Appendix B report original Easi3R segmentation, camera-pose and reconstruction results, including component ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds depth, pose, segmentation, sensitivity and runtime outcomes in Appendix D.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A retain the same attention decomposition, temporal clustering, second inference pass and optional flow-guided global alignment. The added SegAnyMo experiment tests alternative segmentation without documenting a revision to the proposed Easi3R pipeline.

E1.justification: v2 retains DAVIS segmentation, DyCheck/ADT/TUM-dynamics pose evaluation and DyCheck reconstruction. Tables 8–9 add video-depth evaluation on Sintel, BONN and KITTI, plus pose evaluation on Sintel and static ScanNet, substantially broadening task and scene coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 8–10 broaden comparisons beyond v1's DUSt3R-family baselines to depth estimators such as Marigold and DepthAnythingV2, pose methods such as DPVO and LEAP-VO, and 2D segmenters including FlowSAM, SegAnyMo and RCF-All. Tables 8–9 explicitly reuse baseline results from CUT3R; these additions do not establish baseline reruns.

E3.justification: The original full-sequence downsampling and Sim(3) pose protocol remain. Added experiments invoke MonST3R/CUT3R evaluation protocols, compare per-sequence scale-and-shift versus scale-only depth alignment using Abs Rel and delta<1.25, and introduce JM-M segmentation reporting and controlled parameter sweeps. These are additional settings, not replacements of the original experiments.

E4.justification: The component ablations in Tables 6–7 remain. v2 adds sensitivity tests for temporal windows, cluster counts and thresholding in Table 11, a static-scene mask case study in Figure 10, and a SegAnyMo-based segmentation experiment examining downstream pose and depth accuracy on Sintel.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. The additional tables continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–7 retain their values, while Tables 8–11 add extensive results. Under Table 9's newly reported protocol, Easi3Rmonst3r and MonST3R have ScanNet ATEs of 0.061 and 0.077, but TUM ATEs of 0.105 and 0.098. Table 11 reports DAVIS-16 JM of 76.0 at window size 3 versus 70.7 at the default 5. Appendix D also adds SegAnyMo outcomes and runtime measurements of 0.31 versus 0.33 FPS for Easi3R and MonST3R.

T1.justification: Equations 1–16 and the associated definitions and mathematical reasoning are unchanged. Figure 3's caption corrects a reference-view superscript from b to a, aligning it with existing notation without changing the formulation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contribution: training-free inference-time attention adaptation for dynamic segmentation, camera pose and 4D reconstruction. Their principal performance and efficiency claims are unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix D and Figure 10 newly explain static-scene pose benefits through reweighting low-confidence regions, extending the interpretation beyond suppressing dynamic objects. Appendix C's limitations concerning inaccurate backbone depth, boundary floaters and unresolved per-view depth correction remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly discloses the default temporal window of 5 and specifies an NVIDIA RTX 4090 and 512×144 image resolution for the runtime comparison. The 64-cluster setting and Otsu thresholding were already documented in Appendix A. Project access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the bibliography retain the same works. Appendix D and Table 10 add explicit positioning of Easi3R as an image-only, zero-shot alternative alongside supervised and unsupervised 2D segmentation methods.

P1.justification: v2 makes limited spelling, punctuation and affiliation edits and adds labelled paragraphs within Appendix D; the main narrative and section order remain. Appendix B also incorrectly changes its attention-component ablation reference from Table 6 to Table 11, although that analysis remains in Table 6.

P2.justification: Four new appendix tables introduce depth-alignment groups, broader pose and segmentation comparisons, and parameter-sensitivity displays; Figure 10 adds static-scene mask examples. This substantially expands the quantitative presentation. Original Figures 10–12 are retained as Figures 11–13, with existing displays otherwise essentially unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added evaluations test applicability to static scenes and additional protocols, expose parameter sensitivity, and quantify the claimed small runtime overhead. These improve the evidence available for assessing generality and efficiency. The gain is limited by sparse protocol and metric explanations, little interpretation of the unfavorable TUM results in Table 9, and the incorrect Table 11 cross-reference introduced in Appendix B.
